13813-the-common-law:
Robert W. Chambers set this novel in the New York art world of the early 1900s. A young artist hires a model, and their working friendship grows into love. The title points to common-law marriage: a bond formed by living together, not by ceremony. Society, family, and the law all press on the couple.

Chambers follows studio life, portrait sittings, and the talk of artists and patrons. The heroine must weigh independence against reputation. The hero must choose between ambition and loyalty. Melodrama and sentiment carry the plot, with New York as a vivid backdrop. The novel shows popular romance before the First World War.
1758-marjorie-daw:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich tells this short novel entirely in letters, opening with Dr. Dillon writing to Edward Delaney about his friend Flemming, laid up on a sofa near Rye, New Hampshire. Flemming falls in love by letter with Marjorie Daw, a bright young woman at the Seashell House, and the correspondence grows warmer with every exchange.

The twist, when it comes, turns on who Marjorie really is, and Aldrich plays it with a light hand. The book is a summer trifle in the best sense: seaside hotels, clever girls, and a romance conducted on paper. Its final reveal asks the reader to laugh at the lover and at himself.
19301-extracts-from-a-journal-of-a-voyag:
The Bishop of Newfoundland wrote these extracts from a journal of a voyage of visitation in the Hawk in 1859, printed for the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel. The church ship visits harbours, confirms, and preaches along a rugged coast, with a wide table of places at the end. The tone is earnest and pastoral.

At Little Coney Arm no boat comes off, houses stand empty, and only an old man with women and children remains to pilot the ship. Tides drift her toward Great Coney Arm until a breeze saves the day. Readers get a vivid missionary journal of sea, faith, and scattered settlements.
19535-george-bernard-shaw:
Gilbert K. Chesterton wrote this study of George Bernard Shaw, released by a New York publisher in the early nineteen hundreds. Chesterton opens with a joke: most people say they agree with Shaw or do not understand him, while he alone understands him and does not agree.

Later chapters take on the censor, who feared Shaw less for baring private life than for baring public life. Chesterton's book is a friendly duel, praising Shaw's force while answering his ideas, and it remains a lively door into both writers. Chesterton also reads Shaw as Puritan and as philosopher, tracing the preacher in the playwright.
2028-the-yellow-claw:
Sax Rohmer sets a London thriller around the death of a woman in civet furs and the shadow of Mr. King, a hidden master of crime. Inspector Dunbar and the French detective Gaston Max pursue clues through Soho studios, opium dens, and Paris streets. Rohmer followed his Fu Manchu books with Gaston Max, a French detective who matches wits with London crime.

The Yellow Claw's network, its catacombs and golden dragon cave, gives Rohmer room for the exotic menace his readers expected. The plot moves fast, the villains are vivid, and the mystery holds until Max reports his progress near the end. The opium dens and Paris raids give the tale its exotic colour, while Dunbar grounds it in police work.
22146-de-turkey-and-de-law:
Zora Neale Hurston wrote De Turkey and de Law, a comedy in three acts, from the Black life she knew in Florida. The play survives in her own typescript, kept at the Library of Congress, with her pencil notes in the margins. It opens in a village street before a store. Children are organising a game: one boy will be the hawk, and he needs a stick to mark with.

Adults then carry the comedy into a quarrel over a turkey and a trip to law. Hurston fills the dialogue with the speech of her Eatonville neighbours. The play shows her twin gifts early: an ear for talk and a folklorist's love of games, proverbs, and courtroom tall tales.
22638-the-straw:
The Straw is a stage play, printed with full directions for its single-room set. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The scene is a farmhouse kitchen: a china cupboard, a door to the hall and front entrance, another door to the dining room.

The furnishings are set down with a stage manager's care. There is the kitchen range with its scuttle and wood box. At center stands a table covered with a red and white cloth. Such plain rooms, in the drama of the period, usually held plays about family strain, illness, or hard rural choices. The surviving directions alone show the play's world in miniature. Theater historians will value the text as a sample of the era's domestic drama.
2373-the-path-of-the-law:
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., later a Supreme Court justice, delivers his famous meditation on what law truly is in The Path of the Law. Holmes argues that law is not abstract logic but the prediction of what courts will do, shaped by history, policy, and human need. The 1897 address remains a founding text of American legal realism.

Its sentences are epigrammatic and quotable, and its view of law as a practical craft still sparks debate. Law students meet it early, and general readers find it surprisingly readable. The address is short, sharp, and enduring.
23791-scrimshaw:
Murray Leinster published Scrimshaw in Astounding Science Fiction in September 1955. Its hero is Pop Young, the one known man who can stand life on the surface of the Moon's far side. He keeps a shack on the edge of the Big Crack, above a mining colony, and takes the colony's stores and ore in hand.

Some say no normal man could bear it, and mention the scar of a ghastly head wound. One man, Sattell, partly guesses Pop's secret but has reason not to talk. Pop alone knows the whole truth, and he keeps his mouth shut. The old man only wants his memory back, and the methods he uses are, from others' viewpoint, gently hellish.
24275-letter-of-the-law:
Alan E. Nourse wrote this science fiction story, opening in a dark, damp place that smells of moldy leaves. Meyerhoff follows a huge, bear-like Altairian guard down slippery flagstones, sniffing dead, musty air in an alien corridor. The guard's bulk, the wet stone, and the close dark set a scene of captivity under a law not Earth's.

The title names the theme: the letter of the law, as strangers weigh it against justice, mercy, and survival. Nourse, a master of short science fiction, builds his tale from that first walk down the corridor. Readers get a compact story of alien justice, where a prisoner learns what law means to those who hold him.
2767-the-devil-s-paw:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens this thriller in a shabby cottage parlor, where two men linger over port, content with company and surroundings. Outside, wind howls over marshes and rain bursts against the windows, setting a mood of unease.

A German spy plot, a secret invention, and a woman in peril draw the friends into wartime intrigue. Oppenheim writes with brisk, popular skill, and the devil's paw of the title touches every life it nears. The novel delights as a period spy story, full of fog, danger, and stiff upper lips.
28650-year-of-the-big-thaw:
Marion Zimmer Bradley wrote this short science fiction story about a Connecticut farm family and the boy they raised as their own. Farmer Emmett and his wife Marthy took in young Matt as a small child, and he grew up working the farm beside them. When a minister helps Emmett fill out a scholarship form, one line forces a confession: Matt's birthplace is unknown, and Emmett is not his true father.

The tale turns on what Emmett has kept quiet for years, and on the duty he feels toward a boy from another world. Told in Emmett's plain farm speech, it treats adoption, honesty, and love between people of different origins as matters of character rather than blood. The thaw of the title marks the season when long-held truths finally come out.
29060-the-einstein-see-saw:
Miles J. Breuer wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Astounding Stories in April 1932. Its note promises that Phil and Ione, pursuing an unscrupulous scientist, will be swung into hyperspace and stranded in a world of strange sights and shapes. The tale opens with Tony Costello, glum over his glass-topped desk, his profitable racketeering days gone.

Tony once redesigned cars for bootleg speed and built secret radios for the gangs of Scarneck Ed, but a citizens' committee jailed Ed and scattered his lieutenants. Tony keeps only his marvelous laboratory and his freedom, under police watch. Readers get a pulp tale that mixes gangland engineering with Einsteinian wonder, as a crooked inventor's tools open a stranger world.
29204-arm-of-the-law:
Harry Harrison wrote this story about a police robot on Mars. Before the Robot Restriction Laws, the tale says, robots could even decide for themselves. Now a big, coffin-shaped plywood box arrives at a Mars police station on the morning rocket from Earth, dumped by a trucker who only delivers and does not X-ray his cargo.

Harrison, remembered for The Velvet Glove and Trainee for Mars, asks how a machine could be involved in law and violence. The robot's arrival at a dusty outpost sets that question in motion. Readers get a compact, ironic tale about policing, machines, and a frontier town learning what an arm of the law really means.
30746-the-last-straw:
William J. Smith writes The Last Straw, a science fiction story from Analog, September 1963, illustrated by George Schelling. It opens with a note that some hypotheses are rational, if not logical, yet not open to controlled experiment. Kessler reports that nothing can be pinned down with certainty after a plane crash inquiry.

No mechanical defects are sure, no sabotage can be fingered, and no murder or suicide scheme fits. Investigators rebuilt the plane so perfectly it could almost fly again. They gathered dossiers an inch thick on crew and passengers, and worked six months without one positive answer. Smith turns an air crash without a cause into a tense puzzle about evidence and belief.
31512-the-coming-of-the-law:
Charles Alden Seltzer's western novel The Coming of the Law, published by the A. L. Burt Company with first printing in August 1912, opens with the arrival of a man. Seltzer, author of The Range Riders and The Two-Gun Man, follows Norton, who thrusts his six-shooter against Ten Spot's stomach and demands to know what he has done with Hollis. Later chapters take up the rule of cattle, a discovery by Norton, the Circle Bar, and the girl of Dry Bottom.

The title states the theme: law arriving in a country ruled by cattle interests and guns. Norton stands at the center of that struggle, as order confronts old power. Seltzer writes the classic western of his generation, with clear heroes, villains, and a heroine. Readers of western fiction will find a brisk, well-built example of the form.
31778-the-draw:
Jerome Bixby's short story, printed in Amazing Stories in March 1954, is narrated by Joe Doolin, a cowhand for old Farrel at the Lazy F beyond the Pass. Doolin says nothing exciting ever happened to him until the day he rode through the Pass and saw young Buck Tarrant's draw.

Buck could shoot well once his gun was in his hand, putting a bullet where he wanted it at twenty paces. He could not draw to save his life. Readers get a western tale built on that single puzzle: a gunman whose secret is that he does not even have to reach for his weapon.
32168-an-introduction-to-the-philosophy-:
Roscoe Pound's An Introduction to the Philosophy of Law, published by Yale University Press in New Haven and Humphrey Milford in London, gathers addresses delivered in the William L. Storrs Lecture Series in 1921 before the Yale Law School. First published in May 1922, it was reprinted in December 1924, May 1925, and April 1930. Pound dedicates the book to Joseph Henry Beale, in grateful acknowledgment of many obligations.

The volume is the second work published under the Yale imprint in memory of Arthur P. McKinstry, who died in New York City on July 21, 1921. Born in Winnebago City, Minnesota, in 1881, McKinstry graduated from Yale College in 1905 and from Yale Law School in 1907, at the head of his class. Readers get a leading American jurist's lectures on what law is for, delivered to law students and printed for a wider legal public.
32170-the-last-cruise-of-the-saginaw:
George H. Read's The Last Cruise of the Saginaw, published in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in February 1912, tells of the wreck of the United States Navy ship Saginaw. Read, pay inspector in the navy, retired, illustrates it from sketches by Lieutenant Commander Montgomery Sicard and from contemporary photographs. Only a hundred and fifty copies of the first edition were printed and bound uncut with a paper label.

Read dedicates the book to the memory of the brave men who died trying to bring relief to their shipwrecked comrades. A prefatory letter calls his account deeply interesting, naming the wreck of the Saginaw and Lieutenant Talbot's loss, and notes General Cutter's approval for carrying the manuscript to Boston. Readers get a naval wreck narrative, told by an officer and framed by the relief effort that cost more lives.
33302-the-future-of-international-law:
L. Oppenheim's pamphlet, issued by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, asks where international law is headed. Oppenheim, Whewell Professor at Cambridge and a member of the Institute of International Law, writes as both scholar and statesman, weighing how law can bind nations that still settle disputes by force. His theme is hope tempered by realism: law grows, but only as states learn to trust it.

The pamphlet is short and lucid, made for readers who follow world affairs. It suits students of law and diplomacy, and all who wonder whether rules can tame war. Oppenheim's voice is calm and learned, and his questions, posed before the Great War's full lessons were known, still speak to debates about peace, courts, and the limits of law.
6566-thaddeus-of-warsaw:
Jane Porter tells of Thaddeus, a Polish hero caught in war, exile, and the loss of his home, in a tale that won her wide fame after The Scottish Chiefs. Her new preface speaks straight to friendly readers, in a warm, frank letter, and explains why she revised the book for a fresh series of standard novels. She seeks readers who like a tale of honor kept under hard trial.

The novel moves through courts, camps, and quiet rooms where love and duty pull against each other. Porter keeps the hero noble and the feeling high, in the style of her day, with war as a test rather than a thrill. Thaddeus of Warsaw is a long, earnest romance of a man who loses much yet holds his name clean.
8103-moral-philosophy-ethics-deontology-:
Joseph Rickaby, S. J. , wrote this manual of moral philosophy covering ethics, deontology, and natural law, published with the usual Catholic approvals. The preface to the 1905 edition notes that the manual had enjoyed fifteen years of popularity. And that this edition changes neither pagination nor printed text, so that earlier copies stay in use. Rickaby presents the Thomist account of moral action: human acts, law, conscience, virtue, and duty.

The book served seminaries and Catholic colleges as a standard textbook, setting out moral reasoning in clear, scholastic order. Its language is technical, but its aim is practical: to train judgment about right and wrong. For students of Catholic moral theology, it remains a classic statement of the tradition before the changes of the later twentieth century.
8394-the-doings-of-raffles-haw:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this novel about a man who can make gold, and what wealth does to him. Robert McIntyre, a young man in Staffordshire, meets Raffles Haw, a mysterious tenant of a new hall, who turns out to hold a secret that makes him the richest man on earth. Haw pours money into charity, art, and grand schemes, and watches each gift curdle.

The novel asks whether unlimited wealth can buy happiness or goodness, and answers with a slow tragedy. Doyle, between Sherlock Holmes stories, used the tale to moralize on money, a theme he returned to often. Readers get a Victorian fable, part mystery, part sermon, with a secret at its center that Haw guards to the end.
8638-jack-in-the-forecastle-or-incidents:
John Sherburne Sleeper, born near the close of the eighteenth century, tells his early life at sea under the name Hawser Martingale. He was born in a village on the Merrimack in Massachusetts, descended from English ancestors who crossed in the mid-seventeenth century, for adventure or for religion, no one now knows. From that quiet start, the book follows a boy into the forecastle, the sailors' quarters forward of the mast.

Farewell to New England opens a string of incidents: voyages, storms, ports, and the rough education of a young sailor. Sleeper writes late in life, looking back on a seafaring America that was already passing. Readers of sea stories get a plain, firsthand memoir, less polished than Dana or Melville, but valuable precisely because it records ordinary forecastle life from a man who lived it.
britannica-1911-anglo-saxon-law:
Anglo-Saxon law is the body of legal rules and customs that obtained in England before the Norman Conquest. Together with the Scandinavian laws, the entry argues, it forms the most genuine expression of Teutonic legal thought. Continental barbarian laws drew heavily on Roman influence, but Roman continuity broke almost completely in Britain, and even the church did not carry an unbroken Roman tradition there.

One striking sign of this independence is language: the Anglo-Saxon laws are uniformly worded in English, while continental laws outside Scandinavia are all in Latin. Most texts survive in a common West Saxon literary speech, natural given Wessex's predominance, though Kentish traces appear in the Textus Roffensis. The long article then works through landholding, courts, and offences in detail. Its closing bibliography runs to specialist studies in English, German, and French legal journals.
britannica-1911-basilica-code-of-law:
Basilica is also the name of a Byzantine code of law, treated separately in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Drawn up in Greek, it aimed to end the uncertainty hanging over law in the East Roman empire in the ninth century. Judges no longer knew which rules bound them, because conflicting readings of Justinian's legislation by sixth-century jurists had undermined its authority in the schools. Leo the Isaurian's earlier attempt at reform had made the confusion worse, the entry says.

Basil the Macedonian took up the task. He formally abolished the ancient laws that had fallen out of use and had the laws still in force revised into forty books. His son Leo the Philosopher then enlarged and rearranged that work into sixty books through a commission of jurists. A claimed further revision under Constantine Porphyrogenitus is doubted by the weight of authority, the entry concludes, and should not be accepted.
britannica-1911-covenant-law:
Covenant, in law, is the English match for the Latin conventio. That word was the most general term in Roman law for an agreement. It often stood beside pactum, a term for deals that settle a point without a court. In its strict English sense a covenant is an agreement under seal. It states that a thing has or has not been done. It can also state that a thing shall or shall not be done.

Land sales and leases give the term its chief field of work. At times it covers any promise or term, sealed or not. The man who makes the promise is the covenantor. The man in whose favour it is made is the covenantee. Classes of covenants run to a great count. Joint and several kinds stand beside them. Long rules on breach and remedy fill the rest.
britannica-1911-criminal-law:
The hosted text opens partway through a comparative survey of criminal law, at the Roman classes of offences. From Rome it moves to the early laws of the Celtic peoples, preserved in Welsh laws and Irish Brehon tracts. Irish practice treated crimes as wrongs met by set payments, with the offender's family sharing the debt. No crime there stood beyond settlement. The survey then follows Germanic and continental systems toward modern codes.

Much of the entry concerns England, its classes of offences, and its courts and forms of trial. It lists punishments from hanging to penal servitude, which replaced transportation in 1853, and local imprisonment. It stresses that English trial is accusatory, not inquisitorial, and run before a single judge. The closing pages compare modern penal codes across Europe and beyond. Codes named include those of Sweden from 1864 and Norway from 1902, with Japan's code built on European and American models.
britannica-1911-gresham-s-law:
Gresham's Law, in economics, is the principle briefly summed up as: bad money drives out good. The 1911 Britannica entry credits the name to H. D. Macleod, who suggested it in 1857. He believed the principle was first explained by Sir Thomas Gresham in 1558.

In reality, the entry says, earlier writers had set it forth well, notably Oresme and Copernicus. Macleod's own statement runs stronger: the worst form of currency in circulation regulates the value of the whole, and drives all other forms out. The law applies, the entry explains, in three settings. Debased coin circulates beside full-weight coin. Two metals circulate with one undervalued against the other. Or inconvertible paper money is issued beside a metallic currency. The short article closes by pointing readers onward to the entries on bimetallism and money.
britannica-1911-haverstraw:
Haverstraw is a village of Rockland county, New York. It stands on the west shore of Haverstraw Bay. That bay is an enlargement of the Hudson river. New York City lies 32 miles south. The village population in 1910 was 5,669. Three railways and steamboat lines serve it. High Tor rises 832 feet behind the village. A public library dates from 1895.

Excellent clay makes Haverstraw a brick-making giant. It is one of the world's largest brick centres. Brick machines are also manufactured there. Silk mills and print works use the creek's water power. Dutch settlers probably arrived by 1648. Nearby stands the Old Treason House. Arnold and André met there before daylight on 22 September 1780. They plotted the betrayal of West Point in that house. A short-lived Owenite community followed in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-affinity-in-c:
Affinity in canon law is a relationship arising from carnal intercourse between a man and a woman, sufficient for generating children. Through it the man gains relation to the woman's kin by blood, and the woman to the man's. If the intercourse is between husband and wife, the relationship reaches the fourth degree of consanguinity, with the affinity degree matching the blood degree. Today affinity begets no affinity.

Therefore the man's relatives gain no relation to the woman's relatives, nor the reverse. Even intercourse by force or in ignorance, as in drunkenness, carries the juridical effect. If licit, affinity bars marriage in the collateral line to the fourth degree and in the direct line. If illicit or outside marriage, the bar today is limited to the second degree. Trent makes no distinction by line, and affinity before baptism still counts as a bar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bigamy-in-can:
Bigamy in canon law, the state of a man married twice in succession, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Strictly the word means a second marriage after a first wife's death, unlike polygamy, or two wives at once, though criminal law now uses bigamy for the second case too. Canonically, bigamy bars a man from tonsure and holy orders, or from exercising them.

The bar rests on an apostolic demand for blamelessness: a bishop, priest, or deacon, if married, must have had only one wife, since remarriage raised a presumption of incontinence. The entry traces that rule from the apostles through East and West, with its exceptions and dispensations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon-law:
Canon law is the body of laws made or adopted by church authority for ruling Christians and their community. The word canon comes from the Greek kanon, a rule or guide. By the fourth century it applied to council ordinances, in contrast to nomoi, the civil ruler's laws. The phrase canon law itself became current only about the twelfth century, beside civil law. The Corpus of canon law stands beside the Corpus of civil law.

Canon law is also called ecclesiastical law. Strictly, canon law means the law of the Corpus with Roman borrowings, while ecclesiastical law covers all church-made laws, even later ones. It is sometimes styled pontifical law against imperial law, sacred law, and even divine law, since it concerns holy things and the good of souls. Its scope covers general notions, sources, history of texts, codification, ecclesiastical law, and chief writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cemeteries-in:
Cemeteries in law surveys how civil legislation now almost everywhere blocks the Church's burial requirements from taking full effect. In German law, as Dr. Peter Lex wrote, the Catholic churchyard as Catholic teaching understands it has been wholly suppressed. The cemetery has sunk to a mere burial ground owned by the civil corporation. Where civil power opposes it, the Church lets her ministers yield rather than provoke a conflict.

The article then details the law in England. The Burials Act of 1852 empowered burial boards to provide graveyards from the rates. Part was consecrated by the Church of England and the rest left unconsecrated, a share of it for Catholics to consecrate themselves. Separate sections treat cemetery laws in the United States and Canadian legislation on cemeteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b:
An entry on Christopher Bagshaw, priest, prisoner for the faith, convert, and a leading voice in the quarrels of Elizabethan Catholic priests. Of a Derbyshire family, he studied at Cambridge and Oxford, took his degrees, and helped expel the future Jesuit Father Parsons from Balliol. Still a zealous Protestant as principal of Gloucester Hall in 1579, he became a Catholic in France in 1582 and was ordained priest.

Back in England, Bagshaw was imprisoned in the Tower in 1587 under the statute against Jesuits and seminary priests, then held at Wisbech Castle from 1593 with other priests. There he led the elder clergy against Jesuit influence, first opposing a religious rule for the thirty-three imprisoned priests, then disputing Jesuit control of the English College at Rome. He took his doctorate at Paris and the Sorbonne, though Jesuit foes dubbed him doctor erraticus, and he died in Paris after 1625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-in-ca:
William Fanning's entry defines a college in canon law from the Latin collegium. It is a body of persons joined for a common object, so as to form one corporation. Colleges of this kind existed among Romans and Greeks from early times. Roman law asked at least three persons for a college. Some gained legal standing by senate decree, imperial edict, or special law. Others formed under general laws, and if they met the letter and spirit of those laws, their rights stood firm.

Canon law took over most of these civil rules into the Corpus Juris. Colleges could hold property in common and could sue and be sued. The old canonists also fixed numbers for other bodies: five for a university, two for some smaller groups. Fanning closes with examples, from chapters and religious houses to the North and South American colleges at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-common-law:
John Willis's entry defines the common law as England's unwritten law, from Latin communis, general, and lex, law. It covers rules for property, inheritance, and conduct, whose origin is lost, observed since remote antiquity. Its force rests on immemorial usage and court decisions, not on written edicts or acts of legislation. Blackstone, in his Commentaries, calls these leges non scriptae, unwritten laws. They bind not because Parliament wrote them, but because courts long received them.

Willis traces the system from tribal custom to state courts, through county courts and church courts, from the archdeacon's court up. Roman civil law ruled the Continent, and Scotland kept civil law too. When the American colonies won independence, they held English common law as it stood in 1607, with its legal and equitable sides. The entry thus maps a law grown from custom, carried across the Atlantic, and still shaping English-speaking lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compromise-in:
Leo Gans's entry defines compromise in canon law as a mutual promise of disputing parties to accept arbitrators' decision. From Latin compromissum, it may arise in elections or in other disputed matters. In other matters it comes by law or by choice. By law, the arbiter holds office by prescription and must take it. His sentence admits appeal, yet he holds coercive power to examine and punish. By choice, the voluntary arbiter may decline office, and no appeal lies from his decision, since parties freely bound themselves.

Compromise in elections works differently. Electors commission one or several persons to name the elected person for all. Form and limits must be kept, and electors must then abide by the result. Gans draws on Permaneder, Ferraris, and Taunton to sort these kinds. The entry serves readers of church elections and disputes, marking the line between forced and freely chosen arbitration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consent-in-ca:
James David O'Neill's entry defines consent as the deliberate agreement needed in legal transactions to legalize actions. Words, deeds, writing, or silence all witness its existence. Completeness rests less on preliminaries than on ratification, the growth of early consent, which gives transactions consistency. Contracts demand consent internal, external, mutual, and deliberate.

Some call contracts valid without intent to oblige, while others more rightly hold the contrary, since obligation forms contracts' essence. Whoever will not admit that obligation cannot make a contract. Error then qualifies consent: error touching the contract's nature, the object's substance, a substantial quality, or a quality deemed indispensable. United States common law exacts no form to validate matrimonial consent. Canon law requires cathedral chapters' consent for certain official acts of bishops. Consent for sinful acts belongs under sin, and legislative consent in customary law under custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contumacy-in-:
James H. Driscoll's entry defines contumacy, contempt of court, as stubborn refusal to obey court orders. Simple disobedience does not constitute it. It springs only from stubborn resistance to repeated or peremptory orders of a court. Church law generally requires the citation, or order to appear, repeated three times, twice in the United States, before a declaration, though one peremptory citation suffices.

Contumacy may arise from contempt of any court order, not only the citation. It divides into true and presumptive, true occurring when service is certain and the defendant fails without just cause to obey. Causes excusing appearance include ill-health, absence on public affairs, summons to a higher court, bad weather, and unsafety of the cited place. Known to the judge, these void any sentence so pronounced. Effects include trial in absence, presumption of guilt short of conviction, and a fine. Presumptive contumacy carries no such penalty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-custom-in-can:
A canon law entry defines custom as unwritten law. It arises from steady practice among the faithful, with the consent of the lawful lawgiver. As fact it is frequent, free repetition of acts on the same matter. As law it is the result of that fact, taking its name from frequency of action.

Divisions follow. By extent, a custom is universal, general, special, or most special. By duration, it is prescriptive or not, ordinary or immemorial. By method, it is judicial or extrajudicial. By relation to written law, it stands according to it, beside it, or against it. Conditions, force, and cessation are then examined. One disputed question is whether custom can change decrees of Trent. The entry is a systematic handbook for a subtle source of church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-definitor-in-:
A church law entry defines the definitor, an official in local deaneries and certain religious orders. Among monks and friars, a definitor advises the head of a province or order, with set powers. Dioceses divide into deaneries, and deaneries into districts, each overseen by a definitor.

He looks after church goods and helps the dean with hard tasks. Rural chapters elect definitors with the bishop's approval, or the ordinary appoints them directly. In old days their chief task was to split a dead holder's pay between his heirs and the man who took his place. The definitor stands in for a dean who is away or unfit, tells the bishop of the dean's death, and readies the choice of the next dean. No diocese must have them, and at times other men do their work. In short, he is a trusted aide to the dean.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donation-in-c:
Donation in canon law is the free transfer of some right or thing to another. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that a gift of hand, such as an offering or alms, is one simple form. In its proper sense, donation is a free contract, spoken or written, where the donor plainly agrees to give without payment and the donee plainly accepts. Roman law and some modern codes give such a contract only the duty to transfer ownership.

True ownership passes only by real handing over or by set legal forms. The entry distinguishes conventional donations from other kinds and points readers to the articles on church property in each country. For students of canon law, it states the ground rules of giving, where generosity meets the law of contract.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fear-in-canon:
Fear in canon law is mental disturbance at instant or future danger. It lessens freedom, so contracts and vows made through fear may fail. Grave fear must be grave in itself, reasonably founded, and executable. Threats must also be unavoidable for the fear to count as grave.

Grave, extrinsic, unjust fear aimed at forcing consent nullifies a marriage contract. Reverential fear with blows or threats can also invalidate marriage. Resignation extorted by unjust fear may be rescinded unless sworn. Ordination under grave unjust fear is valid, but its obligations need later spontaneous acceptance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-bern:
Baden statesman Heinrich Bernhard von Andlaw, born at Freiburg in 1803, was called the German Montalembert for his knightly bearing, honest faith, and musical voice, though a deeper statesman than the Frenchman. A dragoon officer turned councillor, he quit state service in 1830 for his Hugstetten estate and sat in Baden's Lower House from 1835 almost to his sixtieth year.

Twice moving to impeach leading ministers, in 1848 and 1856, he gave up direct assault on Baden's government. He worked to organize German Catholics on common law and parliamentary lines, serving Archbishop von Vicari from 1847 and presiding four times over Catholic congresses at Linz, Munich, Trier, and Fulda. His writings on Baden's foundations, upheaval, and constitution fill the rest of the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-bradsha:
Henry Bradshaw, an English Benedictine and poet who died in 1513, spent nearly his whole life at St. Werburgh's monastery in Chester, apart from studying theology at Gloucester College, Oxford. His writings include a Latin work on the antiquity of Chester and a chronicle with a life of Saint Werburgh in English verse, covering the city's foundation and its kings. A poem addressed to Bradshaw fixes the year of his death.

Printed by Pynson in 1521 and re-edited for the Chetham Society in 1848, the life of Werburgh follows mainly a Latin source in the monastery library. It is the so-called True or Third Passionary by an author unknown to Bradshaw. He wrote not for the learned but for ordinary readers, and critics have judged the verse variously. His work survives as much for its local history as for its poetry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-influence-of-:
How Christian moral teaching reshaped public law is the theme of this history entry. Law is the set rule of human conduct, and a faith aimed first at lifting the single soul could hardly leave so public an institution untouched. Roman law largely escaped the effect, since much of it was compiled before Christianity won public standing. The laws of the barbarian peoples took definite shape only after those peoples accepted the faith.

Slavery shows the change most starkly. Under Roman law a slave counted as a thing. A master held absolute power over that thing, up to death itself. Yet Christian spirit slowly curbed those inhuman rights from the time of Antoninus onward. The entry follows that softening and similar shifts across the legal field, tracing how church teaching worked its way into codes that governed daily life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-international:
Rules guiding how civilized states deal with one another form the subject of this legal entry, which opens with rival accounts of where those rules come from. Some writers ground the law of nations in consent and usage alone. Others ground it in the law of nature applied to nations as moral persons able to bear duties. Chancellor Kent, quoted at length, holds neither view strictly true.

Kent calls the law of nations law grounded in usage, consent, and agreement, yet inseparable from natural jurisprudence. It draws force from the same right reason, the same view of human nature, and the same sanction of divine revelation as moral science itself. The entry follows that middle path through the duties states owe each other, giving readers a classic statement of the field before modern treaties reshaped it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-law:
Law, in its widest sense, is an exact guide, rule, or authoritative standard moving a being to act or holding it back. The sense stretches even to creatures that cannot think or will, and to lifeless matter. Proverbs pictures Eternal Wisdom enclosing the depths by law and compass.

Job praises the God who weighs winds and waters and gives law to rain and storms. Daily life shows all things driven by their nature to steady, constant behaviour. Natural science seeks those universal laws out: inertia, Kepler's planetary ellipses, Newton's gravitation, and the laws of light, heat, electricity, chemistry, biology, and physiology. Such formulae merely state what happens, while laws themselves are the tendencies to steady action planted by the Creator in things' natures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-medicine-and-:
Medicine and canon law traces how the Church curbed clerical doctoring. In the early centuries clerics, secular or regular, practised medicine without disapproval and often gave it much time. Abuses grew, and by the twelfth century canons turned against the practice. The Corpus Juris Canonici bars secular clerics and regulars from public university lectures in medicine and law. The reason given is lest spiritual men plunge again into worldly cares.

Private study and teaching of medicine were not banned. The Council of Tours in 1163 aimed chiefly at monks who quit their cloisters for lectures, with secular priests breaking residence to follow. Honorius III spread the ban to clerics with church dignities, sparing lower clergy and private students, on pain of automatic excommunication. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 forbade clerical medicine where cutting or burning was involved, and the entry follows later rules on surgery, fees, and conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspect-:
Divine law is law enacted by God and made known through revelation. It splits between the Old Law in the Pentateuch and the New Law revealed by Christ in the New Testament. The Mosaic Law itself divides into civil rules for relations among neighbours, ceremonial rules for worship, and moral precepts forming a divine code of ethics. This entry treats the moral part alone.

That moral law is summed up chiefly in the Decalogue. Tradition holds Moses wrote it at God's direct inspiration, acting as intermediary rather than author. Parts of it, like circumcision, predate him. The entry follows the moral precepts through their Old Testament forms into their fulfilment in Christ's teaching. It shows how the New Law perfects rather than abolishes them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natural-law:
Natural law, in its strictly ethical sense, is the rule of conduct prescribed by the Creator in the constitution of the nature he gave us. English usage often makes it equivalent to the laws of nature, the order governing the material universe. Roman jurists used it for instincts shared by man and lower animals, such as self-preservation and love of offspring.

Saint Thomas calls natural law the rational creature's participation in the eternal law, God's wisdom directing all movement and action. Inanimate things receive divine direction in their natures, where determinism reigns. Man, destined to an end, receives direction in harmony with his free intelligent nature. By intelligence and free will he masters his conduct, varying his action, acting or abstaining. The entry develops that doctrine, its precepts, and its bearing on human law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-crash:
Richard Crashaw, poet, Cambridge scholar, and convert, died in 1649; his birth date is uncertain. He was the only child of the famous Puritan divine William Crashaw by a first marriage, born in London probably not earlier than 1613. His mother died in his infancy, while his father preached at the Temple, and not even her family name survives. His father, a Yorkshireman of prosperous Handsworth stock, was an eloquent preacher, strong in Protestantism and fierce against Romish falsifications.

Crashaw took his M.A. in 1638, and the next ten or eleven years of his life rest largely on Grosart's conjectures from friends, registers, and diplomatic correspondence. A life of religious meditation shows in his poetry, and the friend who prefaced Steps to the Temple called him Herbert's second, but equal, who had retrieved poetry of late. His Steps to the Temple and Delights of the Muses remain his known books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-law:
Roman law is treated here under two heads: principles and history. Its principles divide into persons, things, and actions, while its history covers development and later influence. Early Roman law was extremely formal. At first it ran secretly as the law of privileged classes, then it widened into the groundwork of every civilized legal system.

In maturity Roman law tested positive law by natural law, not by mere enactment. Cicero held that justice comes from nature, not opinion. Law was natural or man-made. Natural law included instinct and the law of nations, so widely recognized that universality implied consent. The Romans thus ascribed slavery to the law of nations, though their own definition called it against nature. Its precepts were to live honestly, injure no one, and give each person his due.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suspension-in:
Suspension, in canon law, is a censure that strips a cleric, wholly or partly, of the use of his orders, office, or benefice. This entry traces it from early examples, such as clerics under Cyprian losing income and functions, and temporary exclusion from Communion, through councils that fixed its forms. Neocaesarea in 315 decreed perpetual suspension for certain faults, while later councils show partial forms.

Total suspension takes every function and right. Partial suspension may take orders alone, office with its jurisdiction, or benefice with its income and administration. An unlimited sentence counts as total, while a partial sentence takes only the power it names. Violating a suspension laid for a past offence brings no fresh irregularity, and a perpetual suspension for crime can be lifted by dispensation from the proper authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-warsaw:
Warsaw, Polish Warszawa, on the Vistula's western bank. Is the capital of the Kingdom of Poland and the seat of both its Catholic archbishop and the Russian Orthodox Archbishop of Kholm and Warsaw.

Its Catholic archbishop, primate of the kingdom, may wear a cardinal's red robes except calotte and biretta. Russian authorities forbid him the title metropolitan, allowing only Archbishop of the Metropolitan Church of Warsaw. The entry surveys handsome streets and avenues, the royal palace now housing the Russian governor-general, the Orthodox cathedral of St Alexander Nevsky, Saxon Gardens, the historic Catholic cathedral of St John. The frowning Alexander Citadel, the Jewish quarter near the Iron Gate, Lazienki Park, and fourteen deaneries with their parishes, churches, and souls, Lodz alone counting over 300,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wladislaw:
Wladislaw, or Wloclawek, is a Polish diocese whose founding date no document can pin down. The city holds over forty thousand Catholics. Old historians following Dlugosz credit King Mieczyslaw, baptized in 966, with founding Kruszwica among seven sees, but Dlugosz cites no paper for it. Boguchwal credits Mieczyslaw II, again without proof, and Bartoszewicz, citing Eugene III's Bull, dates it to 1148, though that Bull shows the diocese already alive in 1123.

Others credit Boleslaus the Brave or the Bold, but Gregory VII's letter of 20 April 1075 to the Bold never names Kruszwica or Wloclawek and laments Poland's shortage of bishops. The sound conclusion from papers alone is a twelfth-century founding. Dlugosz puts the first see at Kruszwica, moving to Wloclawek under Bishop Onoldus from 1161 to 1180. Yet Eugene's Bull of 4 April 1148 already addresses Warner as Bishop of Wloclawek, with boundaries fixed by legate Aegidius about 1123.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-words-in-cano:
Words in Canon Law sets out rules for reading legal words aright, so decrees are understood and their force fixed. Authentic reading belongs to the lawmaker or superior; otherwise canonists use doctrinal reading. Words take their usual sense unless the lawmaker plainly meant another. Clear words must not be twisted into far-fetched senses, and known intent beats bare wording, since words then wear his will.

General laws admit no invented exception, and equity beats strict justice. Contrary-sense arguments hold only when nothing absurd follows. A new law changes an old one only as far as its words expressly reach. Penal laws read strictly, never past named cases, while favour-granting laws read widest. Contracts take words fully, wills more widely, favours widest of all. Doubt favours subjects, no word counts as surplus, context rules, and future wording binds only after sentence, not at once.
doe-osti-2609940-particle-beam-accelerat: Particle beams got their 3-petawatt push, and this DOE report covers laser pulse acceleration. The pages detail the beam physics. The accelerator physicists get their numbers. The laser was 3 petawatt. The pulses were laser. The physicists got numbers. The physics was beam.
extracts-from-a-journal-of-a-voyage-of-v:
Feild's Extracts from a Journal of a Voyage of Visitation records a bishop's sea tour in 1859. Edward Feild was Bishop of Newfoundland, and the vessel was the Hawk. The pamphlet forms number XXXVII in the Church in the Colonies series. It was printed in London in 1860 for the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel.

The extracts come from the bishop's own journal of the voyage. A Homer motto in Greek fronts the title page. A wide table at the end was split for easier rejoining, the transcriber notes. Such visitation voyages linked scattered coastal parishes to their bishop. The journal gives a firsthand view of church life around Newfoundland's shores. Weather, landings, and local ministry shape its pages.
george-bernard-shaw:
G. K. Chesterton opens his 1909 study with a joke: most people say they agree with Bernard Shaw, or that they do not grasp him. Chesterton says he alone grasps him, and he does not agree. That sets the tone for a witty, sharp book on the most talked-of playwright and critic of the day. Shaw's long prefaces, Chesterton notes, are part of the man.

Chesterton traces Shaw's Irish roots, his rise as a critic, and the ideas that drive his plays. He treats Shaw as a puritan rebel, brilliant at attack and weak, he argues, on wonder and faith. The style sparkles with paradox. Readers get less a life record than a duel between two friends who loved ideas, fought in print, and made each other sharper.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VVAW_VVAW: Frank Donner wrote about William W. Lemmer, a 22-year-old who worked as an FBI informer inside Vietnam Veterans Against the War. His piece presents Lemmer's confession, in which the young man describes informing on fellow veterans who opposed the war. The case became a well-known example of government spying on the antiwar movement. It shows the human cost carried by both the watched and the watcher.
jack-in-the-forecastle-or-incidents-in-t:
John Sherburne Sleeper wrote Jack in the Forecastle as incidents in the early life of Hawser Martingale. Martingale was born by the Merrimack in Massachusetts toward the close of the eighteenth century. His ancestors came from England in the mid seventeenth century, he reports. Robinson Crusoe and Peter Wilkins fired his boyish love of the sea.

A shoal of light green water alarms the man at the helm in one passage. No breakers show, so depth enough is judged for their schooner. The deep-sea lead is readied as they cross. Sleeper's memoir gives forecastle life from a sailor's own early years.
marjorie-daw:
Marjorie Daw is Thomas Bailey Aldrich's famous story in letters. It opens with Dr. Dillon writing to Edward Delaney in August 1872. Their friend Flemming has broken his leg in a fall. He must lie on a sofa for three or four weeks.

Flemming's temper, the doctor warns, has become something frightful. Delaney writes back with cheering news of a charming neighbor, Marjorie Daw. Letter by letter, the restless invalid falls in love with her. Aldrich keeps the joke hidden in plain sight. The ending turns the whole tale with gentle irony. Marjorie Daw became a classic American short story.
moral-philosophy-ethics-deontology-and-n:
Joseph Rickaby, a Jesuit priest, wrote this manual of moral philosophy for Catholic students. Its preface, dated 1905, says the book had enjoyed fifteen years of popularity. Rickaby refused to alter the text, lest earlier copies go out of use. The title page carries the church's imprimatur and censors' approvals.

Rickaby divides moral philosophy three ways. Ethics asks what moral obligation is. Deontology studies what ought to be done, and natural law supplies its ground. He points readers to his newer essay on civil authority for the chapter on the state. The manual represents the scholastic teaching used in seminaries of his day.
podcast-dannyjones-o3zr0rZWlAw:
Podcaster Julian Dorey returns to Danny Jones to revisit the death of Jeffrey Epstein. The two had not met in person for over two years. Their title repeats a bold claim about Epstein's cell.

Dorey lays out new details and doubts about the official story. Jones asks how a guarded man could die unseen. They weigh guards, cameras, and records that never fully satisfied the public. The episode will draw true-crime fans who still question the case, and it presents claims as claims, not settled fact. The pair make clear why trust in officials fell so far.
podcast-dannyjones-q1p94mLE3Aw:
Border reporter Luis Chaparro returns to Danny Jones with news from Mexico. Chaparro covers cartels and crime across Latin America. He says Mexico alone now keeps him fully busy.

He reports that cartels have seized military-grade spy tools. That shift gives gangs new eyes on rivals and police. Jones asks why so few outsiders are watching the change. Chaparro explains how tech spreads fast once gangs can pay for it. The episode is a field briefing on a drug war that keeps gaining new weapons and new reach. His reporting treats the shift as urgent news.
podcast-tuckercarlson-bET0_ROWVAw:
The newest war developments anchor this tense Tucker Carlson briefing on looming nuclear danger. Carlson surveys reports of American boots on the ground in Iran and offers advice aimed at President Trump. The host presents the moment as a brink, with the clock ticking.

Carlson walks through the latest strikes, threats, and troop moves as reported. He argues that each step raises the chance of a mistake no one can take back. His advice to Trump is to resist the war lobby around him. Worried and watching viewers get a full survey of a crisis still unfolding.
thaddeus-of-warsaw:
Jane Porter, author of The Scottish Chiefs, wrote Thaddeus of Warsaw, a novel here in a new and revised printing with fresh notes by the author. A French verse at the front praises a hero who hates war and mourns its harms even in triumph.

Porter opens with a letter to her kind readers, tied to a reprint set called The Standard Novels. She calls her tales biographical romances and offers pages on how this one began and the true events behind it. Readers get a famed tale of Count Thaddeus Sobieski and Poland's doomed fight for freedom, a book that made Polish woes vivid to English readers of its day.
the-common-law: Robert W. Chambers wrote this novel, but only a publisher's list of his works is present here. The list names The Adventures of a Modest Man, Ailsa Paige, and The Danger Mark. It also names The Firing Line and many more, down to children's land books.Its inside pages are not among what is present.
the-devil-s-paw:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens The Devil's Paw in a shabby cottage parlour where two men linger over their port. Rain streams against the panes and wind howls over the marshes. Inside, fine linen, cut decanters, walnuts, and famous cigars make a small oasis in a plainly hired lodging, its threadbare carpet, safety-pinned curtain, and horsehair chairs giving it away.

The host, Miles Furley, still wears the sea boots and jersey of a duck shooter out on the Blakeney marshes. Furley is a Member of Parliament for a Labour constituency, broad-shouldered and florid. He is a shrewd voice of the working man, fending off passing socialisms with sturdy common sense. He has refused a Cabinet seat to keep his independence. His guest, tall and slim in dinner clothes, sets off the contrast.
the-doings-of-raffles-haw:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Doings of Raffles Haw opens with Laura McIntyre fearing a guest will not come through foul weather. Its contents promise a new hall's tenant, a house of wonders, and then the workings of wealth and a billionaire's plans. Later titles name a chemical proof, a midnight venture, and the spread of a blight.

Raffles Haw is a rich recluse who claims a secret that turns base stuff to gold. Doyle asks what endless wealth does to a man and his neighbours. The tale mixes science, satire, and a dark end.
the-path-of-the-law:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. wrote The Path of the Law, printed in volume 10 of the Harvard Law Review in 1897. Holmes begins plainly: to study law is to study a well-known profession, not a mystery. People pay lawyers because judges command the public force, and clients want to know when that force may fall on them.

The object of legal study, he says, is prediction, the prediction of what courts will do. Reports, treatises, and statutes across six hundred years are the oracles of the law. Rights and duties are themselves only prophecies of consequences. Holmes's famous essay strips law of moral confusion and treats it as a forecast of official action.
the-phantom-rickshaw:
Rudyard Kipling wrote these tales of India in his young years, and the set came out in 1888. He was then a news man in India, where he heard the lore of barracks and hill towns. The tales bear the heat and dust of the Raj in each line.

A ghost rickshaw bears a dead woman's shape on the roads of Simla, to haunt her past love. 'The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes' drops a man in a sand pit of the living dead. The set is colonial Gothic at its most hot and strange, by a master hand.
the-yellow-claw: Sax Rohmer's The Yellow Claw is shown here through a partial contents list of twenty chapters. Inspector Dunbar takes charge in chapter three. Scotland Yard and a man in a limousine follow. Gaston Max is presented in chapter eleven. Ho-Pin's catacombs and the Cave of the Golden Dragon promise underworld scenes. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
